And I'm sure you'll recall that during the examination-in-chief of Mr. Djosan, I quoted certain portions from that document which relate to NATO Air Force operations around Djakovica, attacks on the convoy on the 14th of April, 1999, and I also quoted point 64, where it says NATO initially denied but later acknowledged responsibility for this attack. And I wanted to ask -- or, rather, I wanted to tender that report into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, anything to say on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think Your Honour had already expressed the tentative view that you thought the document might contain material of interest, and in light of that, I haven't focused on finding arguments to exclude it. It seems to me that its only value would be if it's set out in a summary way that was helpful to the Chamber some narrative of bombing by NATO because, of course, the accused's case is that the bombing drove people out. So to that extent, it might be of some assistance to you, and if it contains such material, which it may do, I don't object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Very well, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions. Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, before the witness goes and just to tidy something up, if I may. The Court asked about the reference to Nogavac in my questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Whether it was in the indictment or not, and I explained that it wasn't save for the limited extent we found, and I've been premising my questions on questions of the accused. The Court will find on day 431, between 11.11 and 48 seconds and 11.26 and 9 seconds the passages that stimulated my questioning. What happened was that the accused asked questions about Nogavac, and that was related to paragraph 63(a)(i). There was some intervention from the Court on clarification of what was being asked, and so on. The accused then turned to ask questions about shelling of Serbian villages -- of Kosovo villages. The witness answered immediately with an explanation of Nogavac and appeared to be focusing on the air attack on Nogavac, and the accused then asked questions about Colonel Vukovic, a witness for the Prosecution who had asserted that it was Serb planes that had dropped bombs on Nogavac. So it's not in the indictment but it was in the evidence, and it may be that that passage of evidence is worth reviewing to see how this witness dealt with it. Finally, if this witness is by any chance going to remain in the area of The Hague, it might be thought prudent to alert him to the restriction of discussing evidence in particular with the witness whose evidence has been interrupted as some similar issues will arise with him, similar to those that we've been dealing with this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I still don't understand why if there was an allegation in the "As Seen, As Told" document that VJ planes had bombed Nogavac, killing a hundred persons, why wasn't it in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That I can't say, because I -- I wasn't the actual drafter of the indictment, if the Court will remember. But, Your Honour, there's a great many allegations beyond those in the indictment that could have been made as to commission of crimes, and there are a very large number of factual allegations or assertions that have been made by witnesses that aren't in the indictment but that are nevertheless admissible, either because they are part of the general background of the picture. As it happens or for some other reason, but as it happens here, it appears both in "Under Orders" and also in the evidence of the witness to whom the accused referred, that these were VJ bombs but it hadn't been thought at the time appropriate to put it in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to say that I'm not quite clear on something here. It's right at the top of our screens just now. It says that there was a question, that I asked questions about Colonel Vukovic who was a Prosecution witness and who said that the Serb planes targeted, et cetera. First of all, Colonel Vukovic is testifying now --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... at the time it was Ali Hoti was the witness. I apologise for having spoken inaccurately in reviewing the position. The accused referred to the Prosecution witness Ali Hoti who he summarised as having said that he believed that on the 1st of April Serb planes dropped bombs on Nogavac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked that question of Colonel Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't asked that question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked Colonel Vukovic the question and he explained to us that NATO planes had bombed Nogavac, and here we even have a map from the testimony of Colonel Delic which shows F16R, that is to say that particular plane that was used to target Nogavac on the 1st and 2nd of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. I consider we have dealt with that point sufficiently. General, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to testify. I remind you that you are not to discuss your evidence with any person who is likely to testify here, and I have in mind in particular the witness who will be testifying right after you, Colonel Vukovic. May we have a separate number for the NATO document that the accused has just tendered.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That will be D323.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the full version of the diary and the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That should be replaced or --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not going to make proposals for the Registry and Chambers because I don't know what is best, most secure as a method of dealing with exhibits. It could either replace the original tab and all go in there together or it could be given a new number, as is likely to be most convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May we have a new number, then, for that Prosecution Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll replace the previous tab with the new document, but only those parts that were referred to; and those parts that are not translated will be marked for identification. Let the witness Colonel Vukovic be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Colonel, you remain subject to the declaration you made. We'll sit, in light of the witness's health condition, for one hour and then break, and resume after the 20-minute interval. Mr. Milosevic. Examined by Mr. Milosevic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 63 we have allegations of deportation, and paragraph 66 relates to murder, but they both allege the same. I will tell you what both of them say. Namely, it says that on the 27th of April --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we please have a precise reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the interpreters are asking, and so am I, for a precise reference.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 63(a)(i) and 66(i) relate to what I'm just quoting, namely that: "Forces of the FRY and Serbia launched a great offensive in Carragojs and Trava, intending to expel the population from that area." And the text is identical in paragraph 63 and 64.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What can you say, Colonel, about these allegations?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that they are not true; namely, that there was no large offensive. I engaged only a smaller part of my unit: Three rifle platoons, one platoon of military police, a medical unit, and part of the communications unit. All in all, about a hundred men. I know that my neighbour on the right wing had 40 to 50 men, not more. My neighbour on the left wing, Combat Group 2, could have had about a hundred men from -- that was from the 125th Brigade. So we cannot talk about a large offensive. Our immediate task -- in fact, security was provided by MUP on the Djakovica-Pec road. I don't know how many men they had engaged, but it cannot be said by any means that it was a large offensive. Incidentally, the term "offensive" can be used and makes sense only when strategic groups are engaged. As for this expulsion of civilians, I have already spoken about that. I said that the army never expelled the population, and that is true of this case as well. What was going on was an anti-terrorist action and that alone. And I can remind you that on the 29th of April, a ground part of the aggression took place on the Kosare axis. In parallel with that, terrorist forces reappeared in our rear, specifically in the broader area of Racaj village. That is why the corps command issued a decision to organise and mount this anti-terrorist action for the sole purpose of neutralising terrorist activity in our rear, to secure safe passage along roads, including Djakovica-Junik road in this case and Djakovica-Pec. Therefore, the sole purpose of that operation was to neutralise Siptar terrorist forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware if during that anti-terrorist action there was any expulsion of civilians?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know of any expulsions at all. There were refugees on the 27th as well as on the 28th and partially on the 29th of April, but they were fleeing from Pec municipality. Namely, along that road passing by my units people were passing from Pec, and there was no combat activity in that area at the time except for NATO airstrikes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you at that time on the 27th and the 28th of April?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's more convenient to show that on the map, if you allow me. The map for that May operation exists, although it's not from the period when that anti-terrorist action took place. The map was done subsequently, but it reflects the actual state of affairs. I have it under number 21. I have a black and white copy only, and it would be better to have a colour map because there are many things that we can't see on the black and white version.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we could have the corresponding Delic, I imagine it is, exhibit number, we may be able to find an original in colour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether the map was introduced through General Djosan, because part of his unit is shown here as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is among Colonel Vukovic's exhibits on the list of admitted evidence, a number 21, and it was introduced through General Djosan under tab 29.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 320. You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you found the map?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The map has been placed on the ELMO. Here in the southern part you see the disposition of my battalion partly in defence. We have explained this map before. Part of my unit was in the blockade line on the left bank of Renik river, along the fringes of Korenica village. Posavoja [phoen] Meja-Orize village, about a kilometre away, and trig point 421, around village Kodra and Kikes. As I said, three rifle platoons and one platoon of the military police. My command post for that anti-terrorist action was in an abandoned house on the road between Djakovica town and Korenica village, and that's where I was on the 27th and the 28th of April. Some smaller forces, part of my unit, remained there also on the 29th and the 30th to control the territory.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to draw your attention that the witness did not mention any village called Posavoja. I don't know how this came to be recorded. He was just explaining where his forces were at the time, and I would like this to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, further on in the same paragraph, it says that a large number of members of the forces of the FRY and Serbia were used and several check points were set up. Throughout that day, villagers left their homes under direct threat from the forces of the FRY and Serbia and joined several convoys of refugees.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already answered that question. We did not engage large forces. In fact, in this anti-terrorist action, the army did not have any assignment or task and did not set up any checkpoints. We can see on the map, and I know from remembering my task, that it was our assignment to take up positions on the line of blockade and not to allow terrorists to pull out along two axes. One axis was Racaj village, Korenica, and further on towards the border with Albania. And the second axis was from Racaj village towards Djakovica town. That's at least the task that my unit received. So there were no checkpoints. The only checkpoint was permanently in Brekovac village on the bridge at the very entrance to Djakovica. It was a mixed checkpoint. MUP members checked civilians and MUP members, whereas my military police organs exclusively checked members of the army and the military traffic that took place, according to the assignment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have explained that. But is it true that villagers left their homes under direct threat from the forces of the FRY and Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've said that as well: There were no threats issued, nor did anyone force these villagers to leave their homes. I can tell you by way of an example. It's not on the map, there is -- there is a hamlet Sufi Dol near Korenica village. I can't remember the name of that man, but his son is Ranko, member of the MUP. He is a fireman but engaged in the MUP. In his house there were ten Siptar families from among his neighbours taking shelter there. So ten families. No single Siptar family had less than ten members, so you can imagine the total number. And they said the terrorists had told them to leave the area. They sought assistance and help from that policeman, and they stayed with him all the time until the 28th when this area had been cleansed from terrorist forces, after which they returned to their homes, and I know that they were there at least until the 14th of June when I left the area with my unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Further on it is alleged that in Meja, Korenica, and Meja-Orize from a mass of fleeing villagers, a large and as-yet undetermined number of Kosovo Albanian civilian males were separated and abducted. Many of them were summarily executed and many of them are still missing. Do you know anything about this? Is this true?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not true, and the allegations are not accurate at all. I don't know who was executed and how. If you have a list or something, maybe you can tell me the gender of those people, the age brackets, or maybe I could be of some assistance. But I assert that the army did not separate men from women. They didn't kill anybody. They did nothing apart from the activity targeted at terrorists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says further on that: "Seven people who were last seen around Meja on the 27th of April, 1999, were later found --" In fact: "Identity documents pertaining to at least seven persons who were last seen at Meja on the 27th of April, 1999, were found on bodies exhumed from a clandestine mass grave located in Batajnica. "

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you have a list, maybe I can give you an answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, here in the appendix there is a schedule of persons killed in Meja whose names are known, killed on the 27th of April. That's on page 56 of the Serbian version of this amended indictment. And I would like this page 56 to be placed on the overhead projector. Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... in English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 56 is in Serbian. That is Schedule 1, or Schedule L -- I. I, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these are the persons killed in Meja in this anti-terrorist action that you referred to, according to the allegations from this indictment.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose this is their age.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look below. It is written in English. That's Meja.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we can see that except for two children aged 14 and 15, all the rest are able-bodied men fit for military service. If these men were killed, if these persons were killed, they could have been killed only in combat. Incidentally, these names don't mean anything to me, but I'm just looking at the age bracket.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you assert that they could have been killed only in combat?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this area, only in combat, because generally speaking we were exposed to a lot of terrorist activity, and we responded in kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever heard the term that I just referred to, that some men were executed? I'm not going to add "summarily," or not, but it says summarily executed here. Have you ever heard of anyone being executed? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is nonsense, pure nonsense, especially those mass executions. I can guarantee there was no such thing, certainly not in this area, and I am not aware that they happened anywhere else. In my unit it certainly couldn't have happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that day did your unit carry out any transfer of civilians?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had no contact with civilians except for early in the morning, around 8.30, and I can describe you -- to you that instance. Early in the morning, around 8.00 or 8.30, at least it was 8.30 when I received the report, here in Korenica village a platoon commander noticed a group of civilians, perhaps 50 or 60 of them, and he sent a patrol, which means two soldiers. There is a cemetery nearby. I'm not sure whether you will be able to see it on the map. So he sent two soldiers to see where those civilians were from and to tell them to go home, to tell them they shouldn't be there. And when the soldiers approached, when they were about 20 metres away from the group, fire was suddenly opened at them and a bomb was thrown, a grenade was thrown. Two soldiers were wounded, one more seriously, one less seriously. The platoon commander sent reinforcements, and the terrorists later probably withdrew towards Korenica village. I know that later, because I sent an ambulance to pull out those wounded soldiers and take them to the military hospital. The platoon commander let the civilians pass towards Renik river and told them to go towards the town of Djakovica because it was the safest place and there were certainly no terrorists there. And that was the only case on that day - and that goes for the 28th as well - that we had any contact with the civilian population. Along the road from Junik to Djakovica throughout the day both on the 27th and the 28th, civilians were passing by us but we didn't stop them and we didn't check their IDs or anything because we didn't have that mission. There were, on the contrary, soldiers who would give them some food and water, because there were elderly people among them and there were many children, and they were exhausted from the walking. But apart from that, there was certainly no other contact. The platoon on the left wing moved during the night about 150 to 200 metres. This is north of the road between Junik and Djakovica. Precisely for those reasons, namely, that civilians who were passing by would not come across any military people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said now that the group opened fire at your unit, did your unit fire then --

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- towards that group?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Only for the sake of the safety of the civilians. And I already said that two of my soldiers were wounded during the first attack. Of course, the commander needed about ten minutes in order to get closer with the reinforcements, and by then the terrorists managed to withdraw to the first houses, whereas the civilians were running towards the military. That speaks in itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That they were not afraid of the army, you mean?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that they were not afraid of the army.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. As for what happened in Meja, and I'm not sure because I haven't got it marked here, Mr. Robinson, the statement made by Mr. Vukovic, which is number 22 in the previously admitted evidence, you can check your own list, number 22, I know that this statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... exhibit number because then it will be easier to find. 22 on a list. If the accused can give us the original exhibit number, otherwise I'll look it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was in tab 31 in Milos Djosan's exhibits. 30.1. And that is Colonel Vukovic's statement, and it has to do with what his unit did on the 27th and the 28th. This is 320, and the tab is 30.1. Mr. Robinson, I'm just checking whether this was admitted into evidence. It was marked for identification and to be admitted at a subsequent date. That is the statement that Colonel Vukovic gave in relation to what the unit was doing on the 27th and on the 28th. And that's precisely what he was speaking of now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. The exhibit number for Djosan is 321, just for correction.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. It's admitted, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Beqe Beqaj was a witness who testified here and he said that in August 1998 the villagers of Racaj and other places first left the village when the police arrived there and in the neighbouring villages. The page number is 9116 and 9117. And then on the 14th of April, 1999, the army and the MUP arrived in Racaj again and the witness says that they ordered the villagers to leave their homes. Is that correct? What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The latter part is not correct but first part is correct. I can talk about this because I participated in this anti-terrorist action. At the beginning of August 1998, and that can be see on this map, although these markings do not date back to that period, when the terrorist strongholds were broken up - and these were probably the strongest in the area of Kosovo and Metohija, that is to say Smonica, and Nec - an anti-terrorist action was continued at Nec, Ramoc, Racaj, Pacaj, Dolosaj. In this anti-terrorist action, part of my unit took part as well. In the early morning, before the action started, a villager from Ramoc, who saw that the army is getting ready to act near Nec, he walked up to the soldiers and asked to speak to the commander. So he was brought to my command post. What he said to me here was that the terrorists even two days before that had left the village of Ramoc and that after the terrorists left, the villagers collected the weapons and handed over to the organs of the Ministry of the Interior. The terrorists forced them to buy rifles at the price of 200 Deutschmark at that, and there were even cases when they were beaten by terrorists, that is to say those who didn't want to buy weapons. He guaranteed to me that there weren't any armed terrorists in the village. And then together with him, of course, the army, in its firing deployment, walked up to the village, realised that there was no fighting taking place, that there were no attacks at the unit and that there weren't any armed people in the village, although there were dug-outs and trenches around the village. This villager, as a matter of fact, took us to the area between Ramoc and Korenica, and in two places there, there were anti-tank mines. So we even marked them. He didn't know about the hamlet of Kocaj, though, whether there were any terrorists in it or not. I'm saying that the entire village of Racaj was populated and that the villagers were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's just get this clear, Colonel. You said the first part is partly correct. What did you mean?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That the army was there. But first I'm telling about the village of Ramoc, and this is a villager from Racaj. I will get to that, if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the hamlet of Kocaj fire was opened. Terrorists fired at my unit. They were neutralised very soon. I think that this went on for about ten minutes only and they probably fled to the forest here and towards Racaj. When part of my unit came to the village of Racaj from where this witness is, the witness who gave the statement, there weren't any villagers there. In the village of Racaj, the military police unit had already arrived, those who were active in the area, but I do know that lists were found of an entire unit. Photographs were found of men in uniform and armed. In one house we found a big warehouse of food supplies and medical supplies. A completely new cellar had been dug and it was well masked with a new door too. On the basis of all of this, I concluded that in this area there was a large terrorist group and that they were getting ready for a longer stay in the area. That is what I wanted to say about the military there and the villagers leaving the village. However, according to the information I received then from my colleagues from the military police, they left before the action started, which was only to be expected. It's the normal thing to do. Then my unit returned to Ramoc and they were there for about ten days in order to keep the territory under their control. There weren't any incidents with civilians whatsoever. As a matter of fact, my own medical doctor examined civilians and gave them some medication. Of course, they returned the favour by giving food, whatever they had, at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. What you explained just now had to do with 1998; right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now I'm asking you about what this same witness said, namely that on the 14th of April the army and the MUP came to the village of Racaj, and then he says that they ordered the villagers to leave their homes.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the soldiers were certainly not in the village of Racaj on the 14th of April. The biggest combat unit in this village was my battalion, and I know for sure that not a single soldier, let alone the entire unit, were in the mentioned village on that day. So that is absolutely incorrect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So we're not going to dwell on it any longer. Xhevahire Syla, a witness here, stated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have I got this correct, that that answer, which lasted for several minutes, was all about 1998 in answer to a question about 1999, or did I miss something?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, just partly, because the question pertained to Beqe Beqaj's statement, who said that in August 1998, the population of Racaj left the village on account of the military and then that the army came in again on the 14th of April, 1999. So it pertains to both.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Xhevahire Syla, a witness here, stated that on the 14th of April mixed Serb forces entered Nivokaz, municipality of Djakovica. That they entered Albanian houses, giving people five minutes to leave them, and that is how a convoy was established that went to Djakovica, and that the police attacked some people who were in the convoy and told them to go to Albania. They were not allowed to leave the route that they took to Prizren, and that was a roundabout road. And then she says that they were stopped near Bistrazin on a bridge there and that the convoy was hit by a NATO bomb, and soon after, that three low-flying aircraft with Serb flags bombed the convoy seven times and killed 70 to 80 persons. I've told you everything now, everything that she said happened on the 14th of April.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the village of Nivokaz, I was not there then so I cannot comment upon this. As for the rest, it is untrue to a large extent. It is correct that at that time the NATO aeroplanes targeted convoys of civilians near -- in the village of Meja, Bistrazin, Rogovo, and Slatzkoj [phoen] and near the Trzin bridge. They started around 1400 hours and finished around 1500 hours. As for our aircraft, well, at that time they weren't flying at all. This is the 14th of April. They were not flying for well-known reasons: Because there was total supremacy of NATO in the airspace, and truth to tell, there was nothing that could have been flying anyway. Now, it's quite illogical, this statement of hers. How could she see three low-flying aircraft with Serb flags? When a plane is targeting, it is flying at a speed of at least 500 kilometres per hour. If an aircraft is flying that fast, you cannot even see it as it flies away, let alone see details of that kind on the aircraft itself. Secondly, any normal person, when being bombed by an air force - I mean, even a soldier whose profession this is - the first thing that a person does is duck, hide in a shelter, rather than look at aeroplanes. This is true, though, that the NATO Air Force precisely and intentionally targeted columns of refugees and that in this convoy there were many casualties. Many people were killed and many wounded. Over 80 persons killed and several hundred wounded. I have a book here that testifies about that crime. If you wish, I can show it here. Among other things, you can see there that the pilot on the aircraft was ordered to fire at the column of civilians. If you wish, I can show that to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a book, "Traces of Inhumanity," and it was published towards the end of 1999. In all fairness, the photographs are black and white but it's better that they're this way because this is so gory, even for us who were there in the area. It is terrible for us to see it again. This witness talked about Bistrazin but first it started in Meja around 14.30 hours. It can be seen very clearly that this was a column of civilians, refugees on tractors, that there is no military technical equipment. On the next page you can see the effects of the attack of the NATO Air Force. I can tell you straight away that first aid was provided, as well as transportation of the wounded and the dead, and that was a very difficult thing to do. It was first done by the police units and then the army came in too. Now, these pictures show terrible scenes from Bistrazin. Here, on page 86, there is a conversation that was recorded between the fighter plane pilot and his command post in the airspace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please read what it says.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Good day, Charlie Bravo." That is the F16 pilot introducing himself. "I am at position 10. Below there is no movement. Request information on red MiGs." There is a reference to our planes. "Charlie Bravo AWACS Michael --" or rather, AWACS in parenthesis -- "go to the north-west, direction Prizren-Djakovica. No red MiGs in the air. Okay. I'm going to 3.000 feet." That's about 1.000 metres. "Michael to Charlie Bravo: You are getting a reinforcement in ten minutes. There is going to be something interesting south of Djakovica. "Charlie Bravo to Mike: We are getting out of the clouds. I cannot see anything else. "Michael to Charlie Bravo: Go further on to the north. The course is 280. "Charlie Bravo to Mother: Keep 3.000 feet. Below me is a column of automobiles, some kind of tractors. What is this? Request instructions. "Mother to Charlie Bravo: Can you see the tanks? I repeat, where are the tanks? "Charlie Bravo to Mother: I see tractors. I guess the red ones didn't camouflage tanks as tractors. "Mother to Charlie Bravo: What kind of strange convoy is this, what kind of civilians, dammit? All of this is of Serb making. Destroy the target. "Charlie Bravo to Mother: What am I supposed to destroy, tractors, ordinary cars? I repeat, I cannot see any tanks. I request further instructions. "Mother to Charlie Bravo: This is a military target, a completely legitimate military target. Destroy the target. I repeat: Destroy the target. "Charlie Bravo to Mother: I understand. I'm launching." And even the spokesman of NATO, the liar Jamie Shea, under pressure from the public, had to admit that NATO committed this crime. But it is only natural that he invented straight away that phrase "collateral damage." And I claim that this -- this was targeted intentionally. This objective was targeted intentionally, and this can be seen from the orders received by the pilot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. We're moving to the next witness now. Zumani [phoen] said that on the 14th of April Serb soldiers entered the village of Dobros. First of all, do you know where the village of Dobros lies and were any of your units in the village of Dobros?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know where the village of Dobros is, and indeed I know the overall area of Kosovo and Metohija, but my unit was far away from that village, so that I cannot be of assistance to you when it comes to that village because I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we're not dealing with that village, but what she says is when they passed by Djakovica and reached close to the Bistrazin bridge the witness heard an explosion and saw that smoke was coming from the convoy that was in front of her and that there were bodies at the place of the explosion and a tractor was destroyed too by the bombs that fell from the air. Is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I've just been talking about. They weren't bombs, they were rockets from F16 fighter planes, to be accurate, but a civilian, of course, doesn't differentiate between bombs and rockets. So that is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. precisely what I was talking about a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, Colonel, count 53 of the indictment relating to Kosovo states that I planned, incited, ordered, instigated, ordered, committed, or otherwise aided and abetted in a deliberate and widespread or systematic campaign of terror and violence directed at Kosovo Albanian civilians living in Kosovo in the FRY. And that with the help of forces from the FRY and Serbia, was executed acting at the direction with the aim of having a substantial portion of the Kosovo Albanian population expelled from Kosovo and establish Serb control in the province. That's what it says in that paragraph and under that charge of the indictment. Do you know -- did you know then or do you know today, have you ever heard about any of this, any sort of campaign, plan, goal or anything of that kind which could even in small detail resemble what I've just read out?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of any of this. I don't know about any of that, nor did I ever see or hear about a plan of any kind. Otherwise, let me say that the army at that time was performing its duties prescribed by the constitution, and that was to defend the sovereignty of its territory, the independence and constitutional order of the country. So that I have never heard of any plan of this kind, or any other assignment at all, nor did my army or my unit ever receive a plan of that kind or execute any assignment which would be linked to some sort of plan of this kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, in paragraph 55 it says that the forces of the FRY and Serbia, in a deliberate and widespread or systematic manner forcibly expelled and internally displaced hundreds of thousands of Kosovo Albanians from their homes across the entire province of Kosovo, creating an atmosphere of fear and oppression through the use of force, threats of force and acts of violence. Tell me, please, is that true? Did you, did you the army, did any of you ever hear of an idea similar to this?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely not true, not correct. My command post was for a time in the area of the Brekovac village, which is at the very entrance to Djakovica. And in that particular village, at my command post there, there were a lot of Gypsies, there were several Serb families, but a lot of Siptars as well. And there was a family living there, if I remember correctly, Cehu was their name, and his nephew Aqir Cehu, or cousin, was one of the local commanders of the terrorist organisation the so-called Kosovo Liberation Army. And he was a loyal citizen, so we didn't mind having him there regardless of the fact that his cousin was even a KLA commander, terrorist commander. He didn't bother us. And then there was Moglica family. Several houses belonging to go that household. I can't quote the exact names of the family, the first names, but I can provide lists of Siptars living in Brekovac, for example. Furthermore, had we had the intention of expelling anybody whatsoever, well, it would be logical to suppose that we'd do that from the area of defence first of all, from our line of defence. And let me tell you this: The population left exclusively the places that were being bombed out of the fear of the bombing, and this Asifiza [phoen] crossed over to the village of Moglica, and they proved -- it was proved that they made the right decision, because that village was later targeted with bombs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was it bombed later?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, during the war there was not a single unit ever there. I used this road exclusively when I toured part of the units at their positions. And it was also used by vehicles, for example, of individuals who went to fetch supplies from Djakovica and that area. And I assume that they targeted it because all the other settlements or inhabited areas is where the population had stayed on, and they wanted to get them moving for an alleged humanitarian catastrophe. Petrusan, Doj [phoen], Krusevac, all those outlying villages. But Bistrazin is the largest place. They stayed there throughout the war. There were never any incidents there. There was just one case, for example, of theft when a tractor was taken unlawfully, and the owner, the lady owner of the tractor turned up and said that the army had taken off her tractor, but we managed to find her tractor for her and return it to her. So that was only incident that happened like that, that is to say an incident involving the civilian population. There was another case that was termed a war crime where a soldier at a checkpoint killed a civilian, but later on we were not able to -- he was certainly not from these villages. We established that later on. But the civilian was unarmed and the soldier was arrested, an investigation was conducted, and all the other steps taken that are usually taken in cases of that kind. And the -- there was a criminal file filed against the soldier, and he was turned over to a military court, a court-martial. And I have the criminal report with me against that soldier. If you want me to show it to you, I'll be happy to do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I think what you've just told us will be enough. Now, paragraph 56 says that throughout Kosovo forces of the FRY and Serbia engaged in a deliberate and widespread or systematic campaign of destruction of property owned by Kosovo Albanian civilians by widespread shelling of towns and villages. So a deliberate campaign of destruction of property, shelling of towns and villages, the burning and destruction of property, including homes, farms, businesses, cultural monuments and religious sites, and the destruction of personal property. Was that part of your activities in any sense whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Quite certainly this wasn't part of my activities. My activities and the activities of my unit I described yesterday or, rather, the previous working day. I testified about all that. And otherwise it would be senseless to shell towns. In all large inhabited areas, especially in towns, you had your own forces there. So who, anybody in his right mind, would shell a town where his own men or his own units were located? Shelling in the broader sense of the word, rocketing and bombing, was exclusively done by the air force, by NATO air forces. I did have one case where houses were burnt by a soldier without any cause. Two houses were set on fire to the east of this map in a place called Damjane, but steps were taken to apprehend the perpetrator straight away, and cases like that didn't repeat themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Colonel. When you said that this was not done by unit, do you have awareness of any single unit of the Yugoslav army engaging in violence of this kind; shelling of towns and villages, destruction of property, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of any of that. I don't know of anything like that happening. Had anything like that happened, I would have to have known because I was in that position and in that locality, and otherwise, I'm sure you know, everything that I'm saying I'm saying from my own experience because I was constantly in the field, on the terrain. And furthermore, I received regular information from my neighbouring units. I would receive reports from the superior command. I would receive reports from my own subordinate units, so that it -- anything like that is impossible. It could not have happened without me knowing about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, is it true what is claimed here, that the forces of the army accompanied -- escorted the expelled Albanians to the border because they wanted to keep their movements under control in that way, up to the border?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you five or six times that there were no expulsed Siptars. Those people who did leave left alone of their own -- if they were expelled, then they were expelled exclusively by the terrorists. They forced them to leave. And they were assisted by NATO forces with deliberate targeting and destruction of civilian facilities. Now, as far as control is concerned, I can speak about my own zone, my own area, where I said that the Cafa Prusit crossing point, border crossing point, which was in the area of responsibility of my unit, that there was an obstruction that had been set up in the infantry sense and in the armoured vehicle sense. And in-depth along that road to the left and right of the road obstacles had been set up. Anti-air -- anti-armoured mines. I'm sorry, my speech is getting worse. But anti-armour minefields were set up, and that means that a mine well had been dug up, a large amount of explosives planted, linked up with the electrical network, and for security reasons, for the safety of the civilians and population during those five days when they were crossing across that border crossing, the army escorted them to the border so that they should not move to the left or right and wouldn't lose their lives on our territory by stepping into the minefield. Otherwise, there was no other expulsion or escorting or placing them under control. Why would I maintain control over their movements, the movements of civilians if they were not armed in the firing positions of my unit? That is nonsense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll take -- Mr. Milosevic, we'll take the break now. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I continue, Mr. Robinson, I wish to ask that the book the witness used while answering one of the questions titled "The Trails of Inhumanity," from which he showed photographs and read an exchange between the pilot and the command centre when a civilian target was bombed, I wish that book to be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, you know what position I take on the transcript, in the absence of being satisfied that it's a reliable transcript, it's not something I can cross-examine to and I'm not sure the book would be of any value. The Chamber knows, of course, the position of the Prosecution already on this particular event. It's not challenged that it's a NATO event. I would invite the Chamber to defer consideration of this as an exhibit until I've been able to take, if I can, a final position on whether I accept the evidence or not. Otherwise, you're putting in, allowing in something that is untestable hearsay where had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And can't identify the source of the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can't identify the source, and all sorts of things, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And you say that it may very well be that you may accept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I certainly accept the events in part because it's not been challenged that this is a NATO event. It's a question of what if anything -- what weight, if anything -- if any, should attach to that alleged transcript of the conversation between the pilot and the base control. That's something that I can't deal with at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think it might be in the NATO report. I don't have my copy with me as I've just filed it, but I think it's in the NATO report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was about to ask the witness if he knows anything about the source of information, the conversation between Charlie Bravo and Mother.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kwon, the source is intelligence gathered by the unit, namely part of the 52nd Company for electronic surveillance and anti-electronic action, which was partly based in Djakovica. So this is a recording of radio traffic between the pilot and the command plane. Also, this conversation was broadcast on several TV channels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you mean that it was recorded by the brigade commanded by General Djosan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The 52nd Company for electronic surveillance was a unit of the corps, unit of the Pristina Corps, and it so happened that one part of that unit was based in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then you should have had the original raw material which contains the very recording.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kwon, I did not receive any material from that company. It's logical that all such material was forwarded to the corps command, to the intelligence unit, where they process all this information, and make it available to other units. The chain of command is such that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In the circumstances, we'll defer the question of the admission of this document until later. Continue, Mr. Milosevic. You're finished?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson. Just a minute. I have a couple of questions left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You explained a moment ago how you let the civilians pass through. Several days ago, you told us that you tried to persuade civilians who were on their way to go across the border to stay, and you said that villagers from some villages near the border had the goodwill to receive them, to put them up.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I spoke about more than that. Here is the village of Zub. It was possible to reach that village by motor vehicles, because further on, towards the border crossing, the road was impassable in several points due to obstacles placed. There were about 30 elderly persons and small children among them, and the villagers wanted to receive them, but they didn't want any of that. They insisted that they had to go. And whenever we asked them why they had to go, they said they were afraid of the bombing in the first place. There were also some people who said they were afraid of the terrorists. And on the basis of that, I made my conclusions. But I can tell you that a systematic campaign of intimidation of civilians was going on, and I can show you some of the leaflets that were being thrown from NATO aeroplanes, and they were meant for the civilian population, certainly not for the soldiers of my unit, because they had no effect on the soldiers of my unit and, as far as I know, no effect on any other unit. Because whoever sees this will understand such -- will understand very clearly that such messages can frighten only civilians, because the army exists, among other things, to engage in combat, whereas civilians are neither trained nor prepared for that. Look at this. You will see a strategic bomber, B52. They were also used to strike at my unit and the rest of the brigade as well in a massive way. And it says -- you can read this. You can see a black bird, which is a nickname for this strategic bomber. You can see this black bird dropping bombs, and it says: "Thousands of bombs. The will, power, and support of the world are there to drop them tirelessly on your unit."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us go on.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's this one too: "Horrible death. Don't wait for me," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say these leaflets produced a strong effect on the population.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A very strong effect, but exclusively on civilians. They had no effect whatsoever on my unit, on my soldiers. I even expected that a power -- a great power like NATO could think of something better to frighten our army, but no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, paragraph 61 is dedicated to the seizure and destruction of personal identity documents and licenses of vehicles. Have you heard of anything like that?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about cases when documents were seized, but let me say immediately that the army never did that, that it was nonsense. It made no sense to take somebody's papers from them because everybody, every citizen -- every citizen of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, if they lose their IDs, can get another, can get a replacement. So it makes no sense to seize somebody's documents. There is a perfectly regular procedure to obtain a duplicate, a replacement. I heard of only one case that happened on the border crossing of Vrbnica --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ordinarily how long would it take to get a duplicate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A duplicate of what? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You just said that it would make no sense for the army to seize these identity documents because it would be relatively easy to obtain duplicates. I'm asking how long would it take to get a duplicate, to obtain a duplicate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry I didn't understand you the first time. There is a regulation of the Ministry of the Interior. The longest time you can wait for a new passport is three to five days, I believe. Don't take my word for it, though, not exactly. For a personal ID it's even less. I don't know about the licence for a vehicle. But the normal time is three to five days to be issued with a document. Of course, if you submit a proper application with the photographs and the amount of money prescribed. I waited, for instance, only three days to get my passport. I did not finish my answer, if you allow me, regarding the seizure of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know about this one case on the border crossing of Vrbnica. I'm saying again this is outside the defence area of my unit, but I heard that a couple of policemen had been taking IDs from Siptar civilians, and they even took off some licence plates from a number of vehicles. The incident was immediately reported to the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. brigade commander but also to the chief of MUP. Since the brigade commander was otherwise engaged at the time, and there was a unit of the MUP close to the border crossing, the chief of MUP Prizren personally went there, ordered that such cases must not happen again. And if I'm not mistaken, he also ordered some steps to be taken against the MUP members who did that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are talking about the intervention of the chief of Prizren MUP when he found out about this incident.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The reaction was quick, and this irregularity was eliminated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me one more thing. As an officer of the army of Yugoslavia, have you ever received an order, be it verbal or any kind, to exert pressure let alone deport Kosovo Albanians?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every order has the same weight regardless of whether it is verbal or written, but I never received an order to deport a single person let alone a group. I can even tell you that I would never execute an order of that kind, and I don't think you can find a single officer of the army of Yugoslavia who would be prepared to carry out such an order. And anyway, in the army it is clearly defined what kind of orders can be issued and what orders have to be carried out and what orders don't have to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any information about any plan of ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never heard or saw any sort of plan of that kind, nor did I hear anything about any colleague of mine hearing or seeing it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about the chain of command in Kosovo and Metohija? Was it operating properly?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where the army is concerned, the chain of command operated just as anywhere else in the territory of Yugoslavia. The system of command and control is governed by the constitution of Yugoslavia from 1993. And if I remember correctly, there is Article 135, which says that the army of Yugoslavia in peacetime and in war is commanded by the president of the republic pursuant to the decisions of the Supreme Defence Council. The law on the army develops this stipulation. It copies provisions from the constitution, saying that the army of Yugoslavia is an armed force defending the sovereignty, the territory, independence, and constitutional order. And in Article 3 it says that commanding in the army is based on the principles of singleness of command with the use of -- singleness of command and subordination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Colonel, I'm not sure whether this is a question that you can answer, whether the chain of command was operating properly. You haven't attempted to answer it, and it may very well be that you're not in a position to answer it. I think that's a matter that we'll have to determine for ourselves, Mr. Milosevic. Let us try to finish the examination of this witness. Do you have any other questions?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have just a few more questions left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge about direct concert and cooperation between NATO and the KLA during the war in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who else could have such knowledge but me? That is to say that I was on the border with Albania all the time, where the greatest attacks came from, where the sorties took place directly, and also where the land forces entered. So they did act in concert; the forces of NATO, the forces of Albania, and the terrorists. It went on all the time, and it was excellently organised. I'm saying this to you on the basis of the fact that I was personally present there throughout the war. I received reports from the subordinates from my own units, I received orders and information from superior commands. After all, this is confirmed, corroborated from my own documents. I can quote from my own tabs that you admitted into evidence and that you have not mentioned so far during your direct examination, where you can see that there was coordinated action between the NATO Air Force, the Albanian armed forces, and the terrorists, those who were attacking from Albania as well as who were attacking our territory in-depth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which tabs do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the combat reports. If I'm not mistaken, that is tab 2. You can have a look at page 189.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did we not have evidence about this two days ago, or was that Mr. Djosan? It's confusing when there are two witnesses at the same time. But we've had very recent evidence about activity from the Albanian side of the border in conjunction with NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think Your Honour has in mind this witness's evidence, and I think it may be a question when the witness was asked whether the action of which he was speaking was from within the territory of Kosovo or from the territory of Albania, and I think it was this witness who gave the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've been over the whole issue of the link between NATO, Albanian forces, and the KLA already in this witness's evidence. I have a distinct impression, and I noted it the last day, that we were going over territory repeatedly with this witness. He's already been before us for almost three times the projected time that his evidence would take. It's almost as if he's here to fill in time rather than to make progress with the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, bring the examination to a close. You're now marking time. We're not making any progress.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, there is evidence of that in your combat reports. This cooperation and coordination, is it undoubted from the point of view of your personal experience and the reports that you received and that you communicated?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely on the basis of my personal experience, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it's now becoming counter-productive. Leading leading leading questions. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you still have other questions?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm putting the question right now, Mr. Robinson. You said that I shouldn't put the question that I had put any more, so I'm putting another one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's a leading question, and I'm beginning to form the view, Mr. Milosevic, that we are in that stage of your examination-in-chief when you're merely repeating yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm at the very end, Mr. Robinson, the very end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you mention all the examples from your zone, or at least the majority of examples from your zone when NATO targeted civilian objectives?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not before this Court. I can give them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: With a question like that, we're in danger of being here for the remaining hundred hours of your evidence. You've surely got to focus the witness's attention on specific events if you're going to conduct a satisfactory examination of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, I'm talking about the targeting of civilian objectives by NATO. Did NATO do more harm to civilian or military --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the relevance of yet another question on that subject when we've had a great deal of evidence from this witness about the targeting of civilians by NATO and the fact that the bombing led to the civilians moving out? What more can he say on the subject?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's just what I've asked him, what you said just now, Mr. Robinson [sic], what else he can say on that subject, because it's a very important subject. If there's nothing else he can say, then I will only refers to tabs 4 and 5 that Mr. Nice indicated as of being of minor importance. That is the notebook of received telegrams and the notebook of sent telegrams. Mr. Robinson, I'm just trying to have this admitted into evidence. I'm just trying to lay a foundation for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Court will remember that these two tabs were not dealt with by the accused in his questioning by any question that indicated their relevance, and I think it was His Honour Judge Kwon who observed that. Thus, they weren't admitted into evidence at the time and we moved on. Whether there is any ground now for finding relevance in them, I rather doubt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He may be able to establish a basis. We will allow you to put a question, a specific question on that subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please look at the log of received telegrams. Just a few examples. Say page 23, on the left-hand side. You have the report of the 2nd -- the commander of the 2nd Motorised Unit, and this has to do with a soldier who had committed a crime.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. Let me find this. Yes. What can be seen here is the command of the 2nd Motorised Company on the 20th of May is submitting information that a soldier nicknamed Brzi, born on --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't have to go into all this detail.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but Mr. Milosevic, in order to make things clear you have to look at the two logs along parallel lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just answer the question and let us move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... 2 in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't hear that, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 32 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, on page 23 is there a report of the 2nd Motorised Company?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then on page 16 of outgoing telegrams, is there a telegram stating that the details of that soldier are being requested? Because it's only his nickname that was known until then.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I'm not very good with all these papers. Could you please repeat the page in the log of outgoing telegrams?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 16, to the right.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The command of the 2nd Motorised Battalion, on the 20th of May, seeks the details of the soldier nicknamed Brzi who had committed many serious crimes. Nezmic Nenad [phoen], lieutenant, is the person who signed this. He was in charge of security in my battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And among the telegrams received, the report of the commander?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly, that he found him immediately. You can even see the time here, if you look at page 16, at 12.10. That's when it was sent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It would be of more interest to know what the crimes were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can tell you that too. The crime was rape. So it was two soldiers who fled from the position, went to the town of Prizren, they broke into a house, where people lived, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's enough for my purposes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't know if it has been translated. I haven't been able to find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 34.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of the outgoing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Of tab 5. In the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's the 10th of May, in the middle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But delivered on the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, I see. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look at the telegrams received, please. Page 31, towards the bottom. The 25th of May, the commander of the 2nd Company, that he had a soldier brought into custody. The log of telegrams received.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He states here that he brought into custody yet another soldier, and he's asking the security officer to come and fetch him. This is another soldier who, together with this other one called Brzi, took part in the commission of that crime. In all fairness I don't have their criminal reports because they are not kept by units, but I have the documents from the war court, and I know for sure that they were brought before a war court and sentenced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 32, that's the next page immediately, it's the report of the 26th of May.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. This soldier who was at the company command, probably no one from the brigade could have come, so he took -- he had him sent to Prizren, to the military police organs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Page 29.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The log of received telegrams. The combat control of the territory. And to the right you have Colonel Delic's order on the command of the territory.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I just have a reference, please? Yes. I found it now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The report of the commander of the 2nd Company, and then on the right-hand side you have --

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. On the 22nd of May, the commander of that company reported that he carried out the combat control of the territory, and he says what happened to the terrorists, and the equipment that he captured, and he also had certain proposals. I immediately informed the brigade commander. I could not do it immediately, though, because the company commander informed me during the night. But on the 23rd I sent my report, and I think that you have it also in the log of telegrams that were sent out. And then immediately on the 23rd, the brigade commander sent to all units in the brigade an order which shows that there are still active terrorists within our combat deployment, and he gives orders to the units to take measures in order to protect themselves from terrorist actions. And on the following page, he commends a unit that had successfully carried out the combat control of the territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, on the basis of these telegrams can a conclusion be drawn on the communication between you as the commander of this command group with the company commanders and the commander of the brigade or, rather, can we see different events linked up and the mode of command as far as concrete things are concerned?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this is precisely what I wished to explain through the question of functioning of the command and control system. I only wanted to talk about the tactical level where I was, but I was not permitted to do so. However, this is an obvious example of that, that all reports from subordinate units come to me, and then on the basis of all those reports, I report to my superior command and the command immediately works on certain documents and takes steps in order to improve the command and basically to carry out combat tasks, namely the defence of the country against the aggressor -- from the aggressor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Just a few things from the log of outgoing telegrams. We already identified one on page 16 where this corresponds to the measures taken vis-a-vis perpetrators of crimes. Please look at page 23, on the left-hand side: Order to the commander of the 2nd Motorised Company to use forces. And please look at the log of received telegrams on page 35, higher up.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So page 23, to the left.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the log of telegrams received, page 35, the proposal of the company commander.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how does this process evolve? What can we see on the basis of this? What does the commander of the company propose? Whose approval does he seek? Does he receive approval ultimately? What is this all about?

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This company commander - I'm going to remind you of tab 6 - received my order, and what happened here was something unexpected. Namely, that the land forces -- the land Operation Arrow started from Pastrik and it threatened my left flank. So the company commander asks me for approval to change combat deployment in that sense where I did not order him to act that way. That is to show that he could not change a single element without receiving my approval, my consent. Of course, on the same day I saw what the situation was and I personally went to see the commander. But although I personally went to see the commander, I had to give orders in writing as well, granting Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. approval to change positions partially. And that was originally the proposal of the company commander because he was a sensible man, a clever man. And you can see in this way the chain of command in the military as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he cannot change a single element of the combat order without your approval, and you cannot change a single element in your combat order without the approval of the commander brigade -- brigade commander, and he without the approval of the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: VLATKO VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. The rules of conduct are very clear on this, when a military person can use a unit independently. And that is to say if there was a direct attack against that unit, first he's going to use the unit and then he's going report to his commander. In all other cases, it is precisely the way you had put it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, just a second. What do you say that all this evidence goes to show, this evidence about the command structure that you have been leading? What are you seeking to establish by it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Seeking -- I'm seeking to establish how the army functions on a tactical level of the kind commanded by Colonel Vukovic. So on the basis of documents, a logbook of outgoing and incoming telegrams, you can see that there is no possibility for the army even to be moved without an order issued, and that every order issued must be completely clear. And it shows the dynamics of the change in position or certain actions undertaken by the army. And also, it shows the reactions, what the reaction is if, for example, a soldier happens to have committed a crime. He can be in a watchtower on the border, they find him, take him into custody, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All of this assumes that the army is acting in accordance with those rules.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It doesn't assume. It proves that the army acts in accordance with those rules. It proves how and shows how orders are issued and how they are executed and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In my view what it proves is that you have something written in a particular document which says that the army must act in a particular way, but surely it doesn't prove that in actual fact the army acted in that way. It's this emphasis on form that is in your case that I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
